stem: Draw the graph of the function $f(x) = {=linear(m, b)}$. Place the two points so that the line is the graph of $y = f(x)$.
solution: Make a table: choose x = 0 and find f(0) = b. This gives the point (0, b) on the y-axis.
Choose another value, for example x = 1, and find f(1) = m + b. This gives a second ordered pair.
Plot both points, (0, b) and (1, m + b).
Join them with a straight line. It crosses the y-axis at (0, b), so it does not pass through (0, 0) because b is not 0.
notes: The objective has no anchor book question, so the parent is the nearest linear-function drill (f(x)=3-2x, lo:u1-4-1); Samuel should confirm or re-parent. All instances have b≠0, so a line through the origin has the right slope and the wrong intercept, which fires intercept-wrong. That predicate also fires for other intercept slips (e.g. sign of b), but the through-origin slip is the likeliest here. slope-sign-flipped, slope-inverted, vertical-line and off-target are left unmapped because the objective has no own misconception for them.
